# A smaller 3D vertex

Status: design, not implemented. Nothing in the runtime changes with this document.

## Why

Every 3D vertex is a `bb::vertex3d` (`code_runtime/source/scene.hpp`), 48 bytes:

| Bytes | Field          | Kept as              |
|------:|----------------|----------------------|
| 12    | x, y, z        | 3 floats             |
| 12    | nx, ny, nz     | 3 floats             |
| 8     | u, v           | 2 floats             |
| 8     | r, g, b, a     | 4 half floats        |
| 8     | u2, v2         | 2 floats             |

There is no w: `VertexW` returns 1 and the `w` arguments of `AddVertex` and `VertexTexCoords` are dropped.

The CPU copy and the GPU copy are the same bytes, so uploading a surface is one `memcpy` (`surface_prebuild` and the upload in
`graphics_scene3d.cpp`). That is worth keeping. But meshes that change every frame (animated grass in the forest benchmark, skinned
models, anything driven by `VertexCoords`) pay for all 48 bytes of every vertex every frame, and in the forest profile that copy was
bandwidth-bound (about 55 ms of a 516 ms frame on merenka-gpu1 with 10 million blades, together with the indices, which #649 stops copying).

Two of the five fields are larger than they need to be:

- The normal is a direction. Three floats are 12 bytes for something that 4 bytes hold with an error far below what per-vertex lighting
  can show. Xaymar confirmed (24 Nov) that `VertexNX` and friends do not have to give back exactly what was written; the original
  had differences too.
- The second texture coordinate set is used by lightmapped BSPs, .b3d files with two sets and programs that call `VertexTexCoords ..., 1`.
  Every other surface carries 8 bytes of copies of `u, v` (`AddVertex` sets `u2, v2 = u, v`).

## Proposal

Split the vertex into a main stream that every surface has and an extra stream that only surfaces with a second set (or a w) have.

Main stream, 32 bytes, two vertices to a 64-byte cache line:

| Bytes | Field          | Kept as                                                       |
|------:|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| 12    | x, y, z        | 3 floats, unchanged                                           |
| 4     | normal         | octahedral, 2 x 16-bit signed normalized, precise (oct32P)    |
|       | 16-byte boundary (SSE, NEON) |                                                 |
| 8     | r, g, b, a     | 4 half floats, unchanged                                      |
| 8     | u, v           | 2 floats, unchanged                                           |
|       | 32-byte boundary (AVX) |                                                       |

The order is Xaymar's (24 Nov): position and normal fill the first 16 bytes, color and the first set the second 16, so each half is
one SSE/NEON register and the whole vertex one AVX register.

Extra stream, 8 bytes, only allocated when needed (decided by Xaymar, 24 Nov: uv1 moves to its own block):

| Bytes | Field          | Kept as                                                       |
|------:|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| 8     | u2, v2         | 2 floats                                                      |

So an ordinary surface goes from 48 to 32 bytes per vertex (a third less to copy and to upload), and a lightmapped surface goes from 48
to 40 (32 + 8, in two arrays whose strides both divide 64).

w is not part of this change. Texture coordinates will later be extended to u, v, w for 3D textures (`custom-textures/design.md`),
and the layout gets looked at again then; Xaymar expects the vertex u, v, w can drop to half floats at that point. One thing to check
then: half floats have 10 mantissa bits, so a coordinate between 32 and 64 only moves in steps of 1/32, and tiled surfaces (terrain,
planes, scaled textures) often use coordinates that large. Terrain tiled 0 to 100 would step at 1/32 of a repeat
near its far edge. So half u, v needs either a float fallback for surfaces whose coordinates go beyond a limit, or a per-surface
offset (coordinates stored relative to the surface's own range, the offset added back in the shader). Half may fit w (a slice or
layer position) better than u and v.

Both streams stay plain arrays of the same bytes on the CPU and the GPU, so uploads stay `memcpy`.

### Split streams or one 64-byte vertex

Xaymar's layout (24 Nov) puts everything in one 64-byte vertex: the same first 32 bytes as above, then u1, v1 (8) and 24 bytes of
padding. The first 32 bytes are identical in both, so the only question is whether the second half is part of every vertex or a
separate array that only some surfaces have.

| | One 64-byte vertex | Split, 32 + 16 when used |
|---|---|---|
| Bytes per vertex, surface without a second set (most meshes, the forest grass) | 64 (today 48) | 32 |
| Bytes per vertex, lightmapped / two-set surface | 64 | 40 |
| Buffers per surface, bindings per draw | 1 | 1 or 2 |
| Cache lines per vertex | 1 | half a line (+ a quarter) |
| Room to grow | 24 spare bytes (w, w2, a tangent quaternion, ...) | extra stream can grow to 32 |
| Code | simplest: nothing optional | `extra` buffer, stride-0 default binding, set fallback |

For the case this started from (meshes rewritten and uploaded every frame, bandwidth-bound), one 64-byte vertex is a third more bytes
than today and twice the split's, so the split is the recommendation. The 64-byte vertex is the better choice if simplicity is worth
more than upload bandwidth, or if the spare bytes will soon be filled anyway.


### The normal

Cigolle et al., "A Survey of Efficient Representations for Independent Unit Vectors" (JCGT vol. 3 no. 2, 2014), compares the
known encodings. Their Table 1, angle between the written and the read-back normal, for the ones that matter here:

| Encoding (paper name)            | Bits | Mean error | Worst error |
|----------------------------------|-----:|-----------:|------------:|
| 3 floats (today)                 | 96   | 0          | 0           |
| octahedral 2 x 8 (oct16)         | 16   | 0.337°     | 0.944°      |
| 3 x int8 snorm (snorm8x3)        | 24   | 0.170°     | 0.386°      |
| octahedral 2 x 12 (oct24)        | 24   | 0.021°     | 0.059°      |
| octahedral 2 x 12, precise (oct24P) | 24 | 0.020°    | 0.039°      |
| 3 half floats (float16x3)        | 48   | 0.006°     | 0.026°      |
| octahedral 2 x 16 (oct32)        | 32   | 0.0013°    | 0.0037°     |
| octahedral 2 x 16, precise (oct32P) | 32 | 0.0012°   | 0.0025°     |

A quick check here on 2 million random unit vectors (numpy) gave the same numbers for oct16, snorm8x3, oct32 and half floats.

"Precise" (P) is the same bits and the same decoder; only the CPU encoder differs: it rounds both components down, then tries the four
floor/ceil combinations and keeps the one that decodes closest to the input (their Listing 3). That is four decodes per written
normal on the CPU and nothing extra on the GPU.

The paper's own summary is that octahedral is the best of the cheap encodings at every size, oct24P already beats snorm8x3 with the
same 3 bytes, and at 32 bits it is visually lossless (their Figure 6 shows hardly any shading difference even for 16-bit encodings
under per-pixel Lambert lighting; Blitz3D lights per vertex, which hides it further).

oct32P is the recommendation: 4 bytes, worst error 0.0025°, and two 16-bit snorm components are a vertex format every backend reads
natively (the hardware turns them into floats from -1 to 1). oct24P would save one more byte, but there is no 3-byte or 12-bit vertex
format, so it would need integer unpacking in the shader, and vertex attributes are aligned to 4 bytes anyway: the byte saved would
be padding. Axis-aligned normals (0, 1, 0 and so on, which planes, cubes and terrain mostly have) come back exactly. The cost is a few
shader instructions to unfold it (one `abs`, one subtraction, a `max` and two sign-aware subtractions, then the normalize the shader
already does), and the precise encoder on the CPU when a normal is written.

A quaternion frame (normal plus tangent in 32 bits) is not needed: normal maps (TextureBlend 6 and 7) build their tangent frame from
screen-space derivatives in the fragment shader, so meshes carry no tangents. If per-vertex tangents are ever added, a 32-bit
quaternion can replace the octahedral normal in the same 4 bytes, so this layout does not block that.

### Cache lines and alignment

Xaymar's rule (24 Nov): a vertex either fits in one cache line or is padded to two, and vertex memory is allocated at the SIMD alignment
of the CPU (AVX on x86-64, NEON on ARM64).

- Today's 48 bytes break it: 48 does not divide 64, so every fourth vertex starts in one 64-byte line and ends in the next, and a
  run of vertices does not start on a line either (see below).
- The 32-byte main stream and the 16-byte extra stream both divide 64, so with the start of the array on a 64-byte boundary no vertex
  ever crosses a line (two main vertices, or four extra entries, per line). That also holds on CPUs with 128-byte lines (Apple arm64).
  Apple matters, but Xaymar noted (24 Nov) that its CPUs are forgiving with unaligned reads: an aligned buffer start and at least
  32-byte alignment perform well there, so 64 is enough and nothing needs 128 for Apple.
- A single 40-byte vertex (choice 2 below without the split) would cross lines and would have to be padded to 64 bytes, which is
  more than today. So the split is no longer just the smaller option, it is the one that keeps the rule without padding. If one
  buffer is preferred anyway, it becomes a 64-byte vertex (main 32 + uv2 8 + 24 spare), twice the size of the split main stream.

Alignment: one constant, `bb::vertex_alignment = 64`, for every vertex array on every platform. 64 covers AVX and AVX2 (32), AVX-512
(64), NEON (16) and the cache line, so one value meets all of them and there is nothing per platform to get wrong. Where that has to
be done:

| Memory                                  | Today                                                    | Change                                          |
|-----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `surface::vertices` (`buffer` in scene.hpp) | `bb_realloc`, the runtime's own allocator, 16-byte granules | `buffer` gets an alignment parameter; aligned growth is `bb_aligned_alloc` + copy + `bb_aligned_free` (there is no aligned realloc) |
| `skin_data` bind and posed arrays       | `buffer<float>`, same                                    | same aligned `buffer`                           |
| Vulkan mesh buffers                     | `graphics_vulkan_memory.cpp`, alignment from the buffer's memory requirements | at least 64 for `memory::mesh` vertex buffers, so the mapped pointer is aligned too |
| Direct3D 11 mesh buffers                | a system-memory shadow copy (`gpu_buffer::mapped`)       | shadow allocated with `bb_aligned_alloc(64, ...)` |
| OpenGL mesh buffers                     | `glMapBufferRange`                                        | already at least 64 (`GL_MIN_MAP_BUFFER_ALIGNMENT` is at least 64 since 4.2); check and assert |

With both sides aligned and the same layout, the upload copy runs on whole lines and full-width aligned vector loads and stores.
x86-64 is the strict case (Xaymar, 24 Nov): an unaligned load or store that crosses a line costs double, two cache lines and two
pipeline stalls. On AMD before Zen 2 it is up to four times (through the slower die interconnect), on older Intel generations up to
thirteen times, and aligned SIMD instructions (`movaps`, `vmovdqa` and friends) fault outright on an unaligned address. So there are no
exceptions: every vertex allocation starts at `bb::vertex_alignment`, every sub-range of one (a place in an upload ring or staging
buffer, a copy for clipped long triangles, a range handed to a worker thread) starts at a multiple of 64 bytes, and every vertex stride
is 8, 16, 32 or 64 bytes (a size that divides 64), never 40 or 48, and a `static_assert` on `sizeof(vertex3d)` and
`sizeof(vertex3d_extra)` dividing 64 keeps later changes from breaking the rule.

### What reads and writes vertices

- Writers of normals: `VertexNormal`, `UpdateNormals`/`compute_normals`, `FlipMesh`, `RotateMesh`/`ScaleMesh` style transforms in
  `scene_meshes.cpp`, skinning in `animation.cpp` (once per vertex per frame), loaders (`b3d.cpp`, `bsp.cpp`, `md2.cpp`, glTF, .x, .3ds),
  terrain, sprites, and the long-triangle clipper in `graphics_scene3d.cpp` (which interpolates in doubles and writes back). All of them
  go through two small helpers on `vertex3d` (`set_normal(x, y, z)` and `normal(float out[3])`) instead of touching `nx`/`ny`/`nz`.
- Readers of normals: `VertexNX/NY/NZ`, the facing test in `scene_meshes.cpp`, the clipper, mesh copies. Same helpers.
- Collisions (`collision_internal.hpp`, `collision_geometry.cpp`) and physics (`physics_sim.cpp`) read positions only: unaffected.
- Skinning keeps its bind pose as floats (`skin_data::bind_normal`), so animation does not drift from repeated quantizing; only the
  posed result is packed.
- Second set and w: `VertexTexCoords ..., 1`, `VertexU/V ..., 1`, `VertexW`, `AddVertex`'s w, loaders with two sets. The surface gets
  a `buffer<vertex3d_extra> extra`, empty until the first write that needs it. Until then, reads of set 1 give set 0 (which is what
  `AddVertex` makes today) and w reads the same default `VertexW` gives today (see the open questions).

### The backends

Each backend binds two vertex buffers for `vertex_layout::scene3d`:

| Attribute        | Vulkan                       | Direct3D 11                    | OpenGL 4.3                          |
|------------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| 0 position       | R32G32B32_SFLOAT             | R32G32B32_FLOAT                | 3 x GL_FLOAT                        |
| 1 normal         | R16G16_SNORM                 | R16G16_SNORM                   | 2 x GL_SHORT, normalized            |
| 2 uv             | R32G32_SFLOAT                | R32G32_FLOAT                   | 2 x GL_FLOAT                        |
| 3 color          | R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT          | R16G16B16A16_FLOAT             | 4 x GL_HALF_FLOAT                   |
| 4 uv2            | R32G32_SFLOAT, binding 1     | R32G32_FLOAT, slot 1           | 2 x GL_FLOAT, binding 1             |

All of these are formats every implementation has to support as vertex input (to be checked against the Vulkan mandatory format table
when implementing). A surface without an extra stream binds a small shared buffer with stride 0 in binding 1, which all three APIs allow,
and the renderer tells the shader to use set 0 where it would use set 1 (the push constant `extra.x` already picks the set). That keeps
one pipeline per state instead of two.

The vertex shader (today `tools/generate_shaders.py`; after the shader-source migration in `docs/Shader-Sources.md`, the hand-written
source) reads `inNormal` as a `vec2` and unfolds it, and `inUV2` becomes a `vec4`. The OpenGL and Direct3D 11 shaders follow from the
same source as they do today.

## Open choices for Xaymar

1. **Normal encoding.** oct32P (recommended: 4 bytes, worst error 0.0025°, a few shader instructions), or oct24P (3 bytes plus a
   padding byte, worst 0.039°, needs integer unpacking in the shader), or plain int8 x 4 (no unfolding, worst 0.39°).
2. ~~**Second set as an extra stream.**~~ Decided (Xaymar, 24 Nov): uv1 moves to its own block.
3. **Vertex colors.** Keep half floats (recommended: they were chosen so colors are not rounded to steps of 1/255). 8-bit RGBA would
   make a 28-byte vertex, which breaks the stride rule and would be padded back to 32, so it saves nothing now.
4. ~~**w in this change or later.**~~ Decided (Xaymar, 24 Nov): later, together with u, v, w, likely as half floats. What `VertexW`
   should return for a vertex that never had a w set still needs a check on the original 1.118 then.

## Plan

One PR per step, each with its own commits:

1. Accessors and alignment: `set_normal`/`normal` and second-set helpers on `vertex3d`, every reader and writer moved to them, and
   vertex memory on every side allocated at `bb::vertex_alignment`. No change in layout or behavior; pixels and tests identical.
2. Packed normal: the octahedral (or chosen) encoding behind the accessors, the three backends' attribute 1, the vertex shader, the
   long-triangle clipper. Pixel tests need checking for small lighting differences; known-good images may need regenerating.
3. Extra stream: `vertex3d_extra`, binding 1 in the three backends, the stride-0 default buffer, set selection in the renderer,
   loaders writing the extra stream only when the second set differs from the first.
Later, with 3D textures: u, v, w (likely half, see above), `AddVertex`/`VertexTexCoords` keep w, `VertexW` returns it.

## Benchmarks to run

Steps 2 and 3 change performance, so their PRs stay drafts until there are numbers from a physical machine (Irkela or Shibela through
the slot queue, never Areldir): the forest benchmark with 10 million grass blades (`forest.py --grass 10000000`, the upload-bound case),
the 600k forest (draw-bound), and Stranded II (lots of static meshes, lightmap-free), each before and after on the same root commit.
